heading: Choose what ty init creates
body:
`ty init` works like a project generator. In a terminal it asks five short questions, one at a time. Each question shows a numbered list. Type the numbers that you want, separated by commas, or press Enter to keep the answer in the question. The questions are: which parts the app has (a client with pages, a server, or both), which Tac languages the pages use, which Yon languages the server uses, where the app runs (the web, macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android), and which examples you want (storage, sockets, topics, streams, an HTTP client, error handlers). A question that does not fit your answers is skipped. For example, a server-only app has no page languages.

Every question is also an option, so a script can create the same app: `--realm`, `--tac`, `--yon`, `--target` and `--features`. When no terminal is attached and you give no options, `ty init` uses the defaults: both parts, JavaScript, and the web. `ty init` creates only the folders and files for your answers. Its web app manifest names an icon, `client/shared/assets/icon.svg`, so each page links that icon and browsers do not ask for `/favicon.ico`. Replace the file with your own icon. Each language gets one small example class, a test unit that calls each public method, and a test setup, so `ty test --coverage` (on Node.js or Bun) and `ty preview` pass on the new app without any change. In a JavaScript or TypeScript app, `tsc -p client/jsconfig.json` and `tsc -p server/jsconfig.json` pass too, after `ty types` writes the composed types. The examples are written in JavaScript, or in TypeScript when TypeScript is the only JavaScript-family language that you chose. A Swift or Kotlin page service also gets a JavaScript copy, so the page works on the web without the Swift or Kotlin WebAssembly tools. A Java page service has no JavaScript copy: it reaches the page as WebAssembly through TeaVM, so it needs a JDK 21 and TeaVM 0.15.0.

Then `ty init` checks the tools that your answers need, with the same checks as `ty doctor`. For each missing tool it shows the exact commands and asks before it runs them. It installs with each vendor's official installer into your home folder, for example rustup, the Go and Dart archives, the Bun archive, the .NET install script, SDKMAN for Java, Groovy, Kotlin and Gradle, emsdk for Emscripten, the TinyGo and Binaryen archives, which make release WebAssembly smaller (see WebAssembly compilers per language), and the five TeaVM 0.15.0 jars from Maven Central for Java page services, which go into the Tachyon cache instead of your home folder. It uses versions that Tachyon is tested with, and it checks each download against the SHA-256 that the vendor publishes (Tachyon pins the emsdk, TinyGo and TeaVM hashes itself). It never runs a command with administrator rights: it prints such a command, for example `sudo apt-get install -y php-cgi`, and you run it yourself. Xcode and the Android SDK cannot be installed by a command, so `ty init` shows a link and the steps. It finds the Android SDK through `ANDROID_HOME` or `ANDROID_SDK_ROOT`. Two server languages also need one library the first time they build: a Rust server builds with Cargo and the `http` crate, and a Dart server runs `dart pub get` for the `shelf` package. Both try the local cache first, so they need the network only when the library is not there yet. `--yes` answers yes for every tool, and `--skip-tools` skips the check. In a project that already exists, `ty doctor --install` runs the same check and offers the same installs.

Later, `ty add` grows the app with the same examples, tests and tool check: `ty add language server py`, `ty add target ios` and `ty add feature sockets`. It never overwrites a file; it stops with TY1402 when a file that it would write already exists.
